title: How AI is Transforming Access to Justice in India
pub: National Law School of India Review (NLSIR) Online, NLS Forum
author: Sachin Malhan · Smita Gupta

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts the practical, workflow-centred direction of the cluster and extends it through a concrete Indian access-to-justice operating model: standards-based grievance management, AI-assisted routing, multilingual access and institutional learning. It adds a material distributional framing—AI’s value lies in changing whom justice systems serve—but offers predictions rather than evidence of realised remedies and does not address verification or jagged capability risks.
qs: To tap into its full potential, the government is rethinking CPGRAMS, not just as a portal for filing grievances but as a framework for managing them efficiently through a system of standards and protocols.

The ideas covered in this article—whether AI-powered grievance filing, real-time legal assistance, or multilingual legal access—are important not because they make things faster, but because they shift who the system actually serves.

st.t: Civil justice: Capacity gains need human safeguards
st.an: The source directly supports prioritising expanded access to justice over elite-lawyer productivity and advocates responsible, open-source AI entrepreneurship to connect underserved citizens with legal systems. Its examples illustrate reach and information barriers but do not establish improved justice outcomes or materially extend the cluster’s human-safeguard framework.
qs: But while these innovations supercharge law firm workflows, this article looks elsewhere—at the ideas transforming justice for the masses.
The real opportunity isn’t just in building ever-larger and smarter models but also in rethinking access and applying existing AI capabilities creatively and responsibly.

st.t: Justice access: Direct AI use shifts risk downward
st.an: The source supports AI’s potential to bridge the justice gap and highlights last-mile barriers such as low literacy and limited information access. However, the supplied excerpt offers anecdotes and framing rather than measured outcomes, and it does not examine verification risks, weak remedies or safeguards for direct users.
qs: Through this piece, we take a closer look at how technology is bridging the gap between our systems of justice and the people who need them the most.
Like much of Mewat, their village exists in an information void—low literacy rates and limited access to newspapers keep them disconnected.

st.t: Public justice: AI access requires accountable adjudication
st.an: The source supports framing legal AI around access to justice rather than elite-lawyer efficiency, and identifies rural information exclusion as a last-mile barrier. Its support is limited: the excerpt does not demonstrate improved justice outcomes or address accountable adjudication, verification, confidentiality or affordability in detail.
qs: But while these innovations supercharge law firm workflows, this article looks elsewhere—at the ideas transforming justice for the masses.
Like much of Mewat, their village exists in an information void—low literacy rates and limited access to newspapers keep them disconnected.

kp.k: AI adoption extends beyond elite legal practices
kp.d: The authors contrast startups focused on elite lawyers' research and case-management efficiency with justice innovation for underserved populations. As an illustration of diffusion, they report that every student at a rural Tamil Nadu law-school workshop indicated using ChatGPT; the professor described most as children of local farmers and fishermen. This is an anecdote rather than a population-level adoption measure.
qs: At a justice innovation workshop in a rural Tamil Nadu law school—well past the temple town of Mahabalipuram—we asked a class of law students how many were using ChatGPT. Every hand shot up.
But while these innovations supercharge law firm workflows, this article looks elsewhere—at the ideas transforming justice for the masses.

kp.k: Conversational interfaces address last-mile access to public benefits
kp.d: The article identifies poor documentation and difficult interfaces as barriers to accessing India's over 10,000+ central and state government schemes. It reports that OpenNyAI, led by Agami with partner organisations, launched Jugalbandi in 2022 as an open-source Digital Public Good connecting everyday chat apps to authoritative information. Farmers reportedly used an assistant built on its stack to enquire and register for schemes through text or voice in their own language; no quantified uptake or outcome evaluation is supplied.
qs: India’s central and state governments run over 10,000+ schemes, many poorly documented.
This open-source Digital Public Good acts as a smart bridge, linking everyday chat apps like WhatsApp to authoritative sources of information.
Farmers were able to interact with an AI assistant built on top of Jugalbandi’s stack,  in their own language, using text or voice, to enquire and register for schemes and services effortlessly.

kp.k: Accessibility requires simplification and tailoring, not just translation
kp.d: The authors frame India's 22 official languages and thousands of dialects, alongside predominantly English legal and government documents, as structural information barriers. They state that only about 10% of the population understands English and argue that AI's potential contribution includes synthesising and adapting information to users' cognitive abilities. Breaking language and literacy barriers is presented as a potential, not an established universal outcome.
qs: India’s linguistic diversity—22 official languages and thousands of dialects—makes access to information a major challenge.
Most laws, regulations, and government documents are in English, a language understood by only about 10% of the population.
Its true power lies in simplifying, synthesising, and tailoring information to match the user’s cognitive abilities.

kp.k: Truckers' legal needs require immediate, distributed human assistance
kp.d: The article describes Lawyered's response to truckers' legal problems, which it says cost the logistics industry $35 billion a year. Working with AITWA, the company expanded a 9-to-5 helpline to 24/7 assistance and, under its BharatMala Project, empaneled a lawyer every 50 km of national highways for physical attendance within two hours. Its reported network comprises 55,000 verified lawyers. These human-service arrangements precede the article's discussion of AI and should not be treated as AI performance evidence.
qs: The cost of these legal entanglements? A staggering $35 billion a year for the logistics industry.
The service evolved into a 24/7 legal helpline, offering real-time legal assistance to any truck driver, anytime.
Under their BharatMala Project, Lawyered empaneled a lawyer for every 50 km of India’s national highways, ensuring that if a case needed physical presence, help would arrive within two hours.

kp.k: Fleet subscriptions scale access to on-demand lawyers
kp.d: The authors report that Lawyered reaches truck owners through transport associations and offers subscriptions based on fleet size, covering over 4 lakh trucks. They state that lawyers speaking directly to police or authorities resolve 89% of cases immediately, with local lawyers dispatched for the remainder. The article provides no sample size, measurement period or study methodology for that resolution figure.
qs: When a trucker calls, a lawyer speaks directly with the police or authorities, cutting through red tape. In 89% of cases, that’s enough to resolve the issue immediately.
Companies can subscribe based on fleet size, ensuring every truck on the road has legal backing at all times.
Today, Lawyered covers over 4 lakh trucks across the country.

kp.k: Preventive AI complements truckers' human legal support
kp.d: The article reports that Lawyered launched LAILA, a 24/7 AI assistant using route and legal-hotspot data to flag high-risk checkpoints and support safer routing. The authors assert that preventing encounters reduces harassment and the legal team's workload, and report over ₹50 crore saved in fines. No timeframe or method for isolating AI's contribution to those savings is given.
qs: With vast data on truck routes and legal hotspots, it launched LAILA, an AI assistant available to truckers 24/7.
It analyses route history, flags high-risk checkpoints, and helps drivers navigate the safest, most legally sound path.
By steering truckers away from trouble before it happens, the system reduces stress, cuts down on police harassment, and minimises the legal load on Lawyered’s team.
The result? Over ₹50 crore saved in fines—and fewer roadblocks for India’s truckers.

kp.k: Centralised grievance systems still impose complex navigation burdens
kp.d: The authors describe CPGRAMS, launched in 2007 to consolidate over 160 grievance platforms, as an example of centralisation without sufficient simplification. They report 90+ departments, 18,000+ categories, over 1 lakh Grievance Redressal Officers and 2 lakh incoming grievances each month. They attribute misrouting and unresolved complaints partly to an interface requiring citizens to identify the appropriate administrative destination.
qs: But centralisation didn’t mean simplification.
With 90+ departments, 18,000+ grievance categories, and over 1 lakh Grievance Redressal Officers (GROs), routing errors were inevitable.
Every month, 2 lakh grievances flood the system, many landing in the wrong place, left unresolved.
The burden of figuring out the right department fell on the citizen who was expected to navigate a series of endless dropdown lists on a clunky interface.

kp.k: AI grievance intake elicits details and routes complaints
kp.d: In 2024, OpenNyAI partnered with the Department of Administrative Reforms and Public Grievances on a Jugalbandi-based grievance bot, developed by Thoughtworks, Agami and Microsoft Research. The article describes dynamically generated follow-up questions to complete complaints and the use of historical data to identify the correct department, category and officer. Reduced misrouting and better chances of resolution are asserted benefits, without quantified results.
qs: In 2024, OpenNyAI partnered with the Department of Administrative Reforms and Public Grievances to rethink the process.
So, the bot dynamically generates follow-up questions, ensuring complaints are properly detailed before submission.
Using past data, it then identifies the right department, category, and GRO, reducing misrouting and increasing the chances of resolution.

kp.k: Next-generation grievance infrastructure targets systemic prevention
kp.d: The article describes Next-Gen CPGRAMS as under development, rather than a completed deployment. Its proposed open-source Digital Public Good framework would establish standards and protocols, use AI for filing, routing and prioritisation, add translation, and generate dashboards identifying policy and process problems. The stated ambition is to use grievance data to address underlying causes rather than merely handle individual complaints.
qs: The next phase, Next-Gen CPGRAMS, is being developed as an open-source Digital Public Good to set standards and protocols for grievance redressal.
Language translation features will make the system more accessible, while AI-generated dashboards will surface trends that indicate areas for policy intervention and process improvement.
By structuring and analysing grievance data better, the government aims to move beyond just addressing complaints to identifying and fixing underlying problems.

kp.k: People-centred AI should redistribute access and institutional responsiveness
kp.d: The authors argue that the significance of these interventions lies in changing whom legal systems serve, not simply accelerating processes. They characterise AI-enabled access as reducing dependence on middlemen and bureaucratic ambiguity while improving institutional responsiveness. Their recommendation is to support more entrepreneurs creatively and responsibly applying existing open-source AI capabilities, with a prospective shift from reactive services to proactive access to justice.
qs: Legal processes in India have been designed for those who understand the system rather than those who need it.
It reduces reliance on middlemen, cuts through bureaucratic ambiguity, and forces institutions to be more responsive.
The legal system doesn’t just need better tech; it needs more entrepreneurs leveraging open-source AI to make justice work for people who need it most.
The real opportunity isn’t just in building ever-larger and smarter models but also in rethinking access and applying existing AI capabilities creatively and responsibly.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Malhan and Gupta present AI as a way to expand access to entitlements, preventive legal assistance and grievance redressal, rather than merely improve elite lawyers’ efficiency.
pts.d: The authors make five principal claims. First, Jugalbandi connects familiar chat applications to authoritative information and enables farmers to enquire about and register for government schemes in their own language through text or voice. Beyond translation, they predict that AI can simplify and tailor information to users’ cognitive abilities, overcoming language and literacy barriers. Second, Lawyered’s LAILA analyses route histories and flags risky checkpoints to prevent truckers’ legal problems, reduce police harassment and lessen the workload of Lawyered’s legal team. Third, the Jugalbandi-based CPGRAMS grievance bot elicits missing complaint details and uses historical data to identify the appropriate department, category and grievance officer, reducing misrouting and improving prospects of resolution. Fourth, the planned Next-Gen CPGRAMS would use AI for filing, routing, prioritisation, translation and trend analysis, supporting policy interventions and improvements to underlying processes. Finally, the authors argue that these applications shift power toward users by reducing dependence on intermediaries and bureaucratic ambiguity, and predict that innovators applying existing open-source AI can make legal access more proactive and seamless.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence offered consists primarily of implementation narratives, operational figures and the authors’ practitioner experience; the article does not present a formal AI performance evaluation.
pts.d: For Jugalbandi, the authors describe its 2022 launch and farmers’ use of an assistant built on its stack to enquire about and register for schemes, without reporting user counts, completion rates or measured access improvements. Contextual figures include over 10,000 government schemes, 22 official languages and English comprehension of about 10% of the population. For Lawyered, the article reports a network of 55,000 verified lawyers, highway coverage at 50-km intervals, physical assistance within two hours, immediate resolution in 89% of cases through lawyer intervention, and coverage of over 400,000 trucks. These describe the broader lawyer-backed service, not measured AI performance. The LAILA discussion reports over ₹50 crore saved in fines, but provides no measurement period, methodology or separation of AI’s contribution from the wider service. For CPGRAMS, the authors describe the 2024 partnership and bot functionality against a backdrop of over 90 departments, 18,000 grievance categories, 100,000 officers and 200,000 monthly grievances; no before-and-after routing or resolution figures are supplied. The rural law-school workshop provides anecdotal evidence of widespread ChatGPT use among the students present, not of legal-service outcomes. The author biographies identify Malhan as Agami’s co-founder and Gupta as an OpenNyAI co-lead, establishing involvement in initiatives discussed. Predictions about systemic power shifts and future grievance management are arguments and development intentions rather than reported evaluated outcomes.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The 2025 article mixes descriptions of existing services with undated predictions about evolving AI and a grievance platform still under development.
pts.d: Jugalbandi is described as launched in 2022, with farmer interactions already having occurred. Its access mechanism depends on affordable mobile connectivity, familiar chat applications, authoritative information sources and local-language text or voice interaction. Lawyered’s human legal-support service expanded during the pandemic; LAILA is presented as already launched and available around the clock, with no launch date or savings period specified. Its preventive function uses route and legal-hotspot data, while the wider service relies on transport-association partnerships, fleet subscriptions and a geographically distributed lawyer network. The CPGRAMS collaboration began in 2024, and the grievance bot is described as introduced; historical grievance data supports its routing function. Next-Gen CPGRAMS is explicitly being developed, with its AI capabilities described prospectively and no completion date. The broader predictions are conditional on AI’s evolution and on innovators creatively and responsibly applying existing capabilities, rather than on a specified model breakthrough or deadline.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal intended beneficiaries are underserved Indian citizens; legal-support providers and public grievance officials also experience changes in workload and service delivery.
pts.d: Farmers and people facing literacy or language barriers gain more usable access to information about subsidies, insurance, credit and other entitlements, including assistance with registration. Truck drivers gain preventive information and access to timely legal support; fleet owners and logistics businesses benefit from fewer fines, disruptions and cargo-related risks. Those commercial savings are distinct from the article’s broader access-to-justice claims. Lawyered’s lawyers are said to face a reduced legal workload through prevention, while remaining central to direct intervention and physical assistance; the article does not predict their replacement. Citizens filing grievances receive help articulating complaints and finding the responsible authority. Grievance redressal officers, departments and policymakers are expected to gain better routing, prioritisation and visibility into systemic problems. More broadly, the authors envision reduced reliance on middlemen, greater institutional responsiveness and a larger role for entrepreneurs developing public-facing justice tools, rather than focusing on elite law firms.
